You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

Test input (5x6):

3 3 3 3 3 3

3 3 3 3 3 3
3 5 3 5 3 3
Wrong attempts used: 0/8. Demo requests used: 0/8.
Reply with exactly one action JSON on the last line.

# Fill intervals between aligned markers

Use when an ARC demonstration shows sparse markers on a uniform background and adds a third color in spaces between aligned marks.

1. Identify the uniform background, marker color, and fill color from the examples. Keep all markers and all background cells outside qualifying intervals unchanged.
2. For each row, find the first and last marker. Replace only background cells strictly between them with the fill color. Do not extend past either endpoint.
3. Repeat for each column: find its first and last marker and fill only background cells strictly between those endpoints.
4. Preserve marker pixels even if a row/column interval crosses them. Overlapping row and column fills simply remain fill color.
5. Validate dimensions and allowed colors. Avoid extending rays to grid boundaries unless demonstrations explicitly show that behavior.

A key distinction: fill the intervals bracketed by markers, not every background cell, not just between adjacent marker pairs, and not unbounded rays. # Infer local gap completion in sparse ARC patterns

Use when isolated foreground markers occur along a uniform field and outputs may recolor background cells between markers. Distinguish local neighbor gaps from full-line bracketing, periodic completion, and broad parity-based fill.

## Workflow
1. Record exact marker coordinates, colors, and background for each demonstration. Inventory only changed cells in the output.
2. Segment marker runs: test horizontal adjacency/cadence first, and separately test vertical or diagonal relations. Do not assume all same-color markers belong to one object.
3. Compare candidate rules precisely: fill only internal gaps between consecutive markers in a run; fill all background cells between first/last marker; fill a periodic/parity sequence; or extend a ray. A short run with two markers can distinguish one intervening cell from unlimited line filling.
4. Determine whether endpoints need exactly one background cell between them, whether longer gaps qualify, and whether one or multiple orientations apply. Infer these from outputs.
5. Infer inserted color and verify palette independence across demos. Preserve markers and untouched background; test every changed and unchanged cell.
6. Apply only demonstrated scope to the test. Validate dimensions and avoid filling run ends or unrelated marker groups.
7. If a submission fails, revisit segmentation, orientation, and extent; do not repeat the same structural rule with cosmetic edits. Request a distinguishing demo when competing hypotheses remain.

## Unresolved recurrence: task-d8a672a1
Eight demos show isolated motifs formed by two opposing orthogonal rails/edges, with sparse interruptions or marks along the lines. Output recolors selected background cells to color 2, not blanket line gaps. Test palette bg6, marker1, dimensions 19x29. Eight submissions failed. Candidate fills made and rejected: (a) fill every internal horizontal gap in marker rows and vertical gaps in marker columns; (b) additionally fill coordinatewise row/column spans; (c) fill some inferred edges from sparse line segments; (d) horizontal gaps only while keeping unrelated isolated vertical pixels. Therefore do not use any simple all-horizontal/all-vertical interpolation or bounding spans.

Demo evidence, indexed zero-based and changed coordinates from background to 2:
1 (17x10,bg9,marker0): (5,2),(5,3); (6,0),(6,4); (8,0); (9,0),(9,4); (10,0),(10,4); (11,4); (12,0),(12,4); (14,4); (15,2),(15,3). The marker arrangement has paired columns 0/4 and paired top/bottom row6/15 with extra row5; fills make a rectangular/rail-like structure selectively.
2 (15x12,bg9,marker1): no changes despite a complete hollow rectangle (rows5-13, cols4-8) — rectangle alone is not sufficient.
3 (30x11,bg9,marker8): changes create rectangular outline rows14-22, cols5-10; added cells are top row cols6-9, bottom row cols6-9, sides at cols5 and10 on rows15-21 except existing marks remain unchanged. Strong evidence for closing a particular sparse rectangle-like frame, while original markers are preserved.
4 (16x24,bg0,marker4): changes only in a rectangle-like outline rows2-12, cols7-19, specifically (2,12),(9,8),(9,11),(9,12),(9,13),(9,15),(9,18),(12,12). Does not fill complete rectangle; row9 motif seems sparse internal markers within the outline.
5 (28x29,bg4,marker1): two missing edge cells filled: (13,6),(20,4), closing two incomplete rectangle-like outlines bounded by rows13/20 and cols3/15.
6 (29x24,bg4,marker0): changes are selective 2s in apparent rectangle-row/column pattern: row8 cols17,18,20,21; row9 col12; row12 cols13,14,16,18,19,20,23; row14 col12; row15 col12; row16 col23; row20 cols15,19,21,22. Several line breaks/marks are included, not generic closure.

Overall likely task: infer/fill missing pixels in outlined rectangles/frames (color2) but selection depends on a more specific structural/marking rule than closure alone; demo 2 complete rectangle unchanged. Do not claim solved. On recurrence request demos and analyze each component/frame boundaries, which gaps receive 2, and whether interior noise/marks encode eligibility. In particular distinguish intentional hollow frames (preserved) from interrupted outlines to repair.

## Pitfalls
- Alternating marker/background appearance alone does not prove every matching gap in the grid should be filled.
- A horizontal pair does not justify vertical fills or filling between distant nonconsecutive markers.
- Do not confuse local adjacent-gap completion with row/column first-to-last interval filling; check whether all interior cells or only immediate gaps change.
- Keep unverified hypotheses explicitly unresolved. A plausible output is not a validated rule.

# Continual-ARC demonstration-driven inference

Use for ARC-style tasks where a demonstration request has a score cost and outputs may transform many cells.

## Workflow
1. Before requesting a demo, identify competing candidate rules and the observation that would distinguish them.
- On each demo pair, compare input and output cell-by-cell. Record changed coordinates, dimensions, colors, preserved regions, and any special object/motif coordinates. Distinguish demonstrations from accepted submissions; recurrence notes labeled provisional may be wrong and must not override live evidence.
3. Update candidate hypotheses explicitly: check whether each predicts every change and every unchanged region. Reject rules that only match visually or explain a subset.
4. Request another demo only if it is likely to distinguish live hypotheses and its information value justifies its cost. Avoid repeated requests without extracting new evidence.
5. Submit only after one rule predicts all observed examples and can be applied unambiguously to the test. If unresolved, prefer the action with the lower expected cost; do not disguise a guess as a validated rule.

## Pitfalls
- Many output changes do not by themselves establish a stencil, propagation, or connected-component rule.
- A new demo should change the hypothesis state; otherwise the request was not used effectively.
- Do not overfit one pair or submit a plausible visual pattern without exact coordinate-level verification.

## task-1ce70170 recurrence: unresolved, cap exhausted (2026-09)
This instance reached 8 wrong submissions (cost cap) after 6 demo requests. Do not treat any test output/rule below as accepted. The demonstrated structure is not consistently explained by any attempted simple direct-panel recoloring.

Test grid (15x11) separator row 7 (0-based), color 8. Upper panel 7x11 uses colors 5/7; lower panel 7x11 uses 5/6. Submitted attempts all failed:
1-2: 7x11 output mapping upper-panel 5 to3, 7 to8.
3: upper-panel 5->3,7->5.
4: 7x11 from upper pattern mapping 5->3,7->8 (variant).
5: output from upper panel mapping 5->3,7->0.
6: 7x11 upper mapping 5->3,7->0 (duplicate family).
7: upper mapping 5->3,7->7 (preserve background).
8: lower panel mapped 6->3,5->6.
All were incorrect. Avoid these direct-copy/palette variants on recurrence.

Six demos in this episode:
D1 input 16x29, vertical divider col14 color9, output 16x14: output is right panel (color2/8) recolored 2->3, 8->8 exactly; left panel ignored.
D2 input 25x3, horizontal divider row12 color9, output 12x3: top panel (0/4) transformed 4->3, 0->0 exactly; bottom panel ignored.
D3 input 26x17, vertical divider col8 color8, output 26x8: left panel (2/4) becomes 3 at cells that were 4, and 2 remains 2; right panel ignored.
D4 input 16x23, vertical divider col11 color8, output 16x11: left panel (0/2) outputs 3 at input 0 and 2 at input 2; right panel ignored.
D5 input 27x18, horizontal divider row13 color5, output 13x18: top panel (7/8) maps 8->3 and 7->8; bottom panel ignored.
D6 input 25x18, horizontal divider row12 color1, output 12x18: top panel (5/9) maps 9->3, 5->5; bottom panel ignored.

Strong rule supported by all demos: remove the separator and retain the panel preceding it (top for horizontal, left for vertical) except D1: there output clearly corresponds to right panel since divider at col14 splits 14 left columns and 14 right columns, output 16x14 and 3s in right-panel marker positions. Re-examining D1: output exactly has 3 at positions of 2 in right panel and 8 elsewhere; left panel is uniform 8 with sparse 4s. Therefore panel selection might be the panel whose values contrast via non-background rare-color marker; demos select whichever half has a rare/different foreground signal and convert that rare foreground to 3 while preserving panel background. In D2 top panel has sparse 4 on 0; D3 left 4 among 2; D4 left 0 among 2; D5 top 8 among 7; D6 top 9 among 5. D1 right panel has 2 among 8, while left 4 among 8, both candidates superficially marker-like, so perhaps a selector chooses one side based on a latent property. Crucially D1's output confirms right panel, contradicting any universal 'preceding panel' rule.

Potential inference: output retains a selected panel with rare color recolored 3 and dominant background unchanged; selector may depend on marker count/geometry or separator orientation/values. Need derive selector and mapping from all examples. Demo outputs largely copy one panel with just one of its two colors changed to3, not combination/mask. Count marker pixels / compare distributions per panel and test which panel output corresponds to across demos before any attempt. These tests remain all failed; no known solution. A request for further demos could help if cap permits; avoid repeating direct panel guesses.
Partition the input into non-overlapping 3x3 blocks. Produce one output cell per block (so an 18x18 input yields 6x6; 21x21 yields 7x7; 24x24 yields 8x8). The output is the most frequent color in each 3x3 block, except cells equal to the dominant noise/background color are ignored when a non-background object color occurs, and blocks containing no non-background colors emit 0. In task-013fba0f the 27x27 test partitions into 9x9 blocks; ignore background 5, output the mode among all non-5 cells (ties choose the lowest-valued color), or 0 if all 5s. This was confirmed on three demos and the test. Demo 1: 15x15→5x5, all blocks output 0 except block (3,4)=8, despite sparse 8 markers; blocks with 0 and 5 noise output 0. Demo 2: 12x12→4x4, output [[7,7,7,0],[9,7,0,9],[9,0,9,3],[0,7,7,9]]; demonstrates ignoring background 5 and selecting the locally dominant non-5 object/noise color. Demo 3: 15x15→5x5, output [[0,3,0,0,8],[0,8,0,8,6],[2,0,4,7,0],[6,0,0,0,0],[0,0,0,7,1]]. Test accepted 9x9 result: [[7,1,0,2,0,3,4,0,6],[0,0,1,1,0,8,7,4,0],[7,8,0,3,0,0,4,8,6],[0,7,1,6,2,0,7,2,6],[4,0,0,8,0,6,0,0,7],[1,6,3,7,0,2,0,2,0],[0,0,6,0,1,6,3,2,0],[8,0,2,7,4,7,3,7,8],[1,7,0,0,7,4,1,0,7]]. Tie precedence should be inferred from demos; this test had no unresolved ties after background exclusion. This rule's initial simplistic all-cell majority/background-5-to-0 guess was wrong because background 5 frequently outnumbered salient block contents; exclude background before taking mode. A later recurrence test (15x15) was solved with the 5x5 output [[0,4,4,0,7],[4,4,7,4,4],[7,4,7,7,7],[4,4,4,4,4],[7,7,0,4,0]] by this method; every 3x3 block had only one non-background color, so no tie policy was needed. Infer the background from the demos (e.g. 5 in the 21x21 demo and 5 in the test; 5 also was the scattered background/noise in test). In test, this exact 8x8 output was accepted after one incorrect earlier guess: [[0,3,0,0,2,0,6,0],[6,0,0,0,0,0,0,3],[6,4,0,6,9,9,0,0],[4,0,0,0,0,0,0,0],[0,2,9,6,0,0,4,0],[4,9,0,0,6,9,3,0],[0,0,2,0,9,0,0,0],[0,0,0,0,0,9,4,2]].
